pages.title: Warriors : The Broken Code #1
pages.author: Erin Hunter
pages.text: A bitter winter brings more than hunger and cold to the warrior cat Clans. Their connection to StarClan has fallen silent, leaving the living cats without the guidance of their ancestors. One young ShadowClan apprentice still hears voices, but the messages point toward a new danger within the Clans themselves. Lost Stars opens The Broken Code, a Warriors story about loyalty, inherited rules and the uncertainty of following signs that others cannot hear.

pages.title: The Diary of Frida Kahlo
pages.author: Frida Kahlo
pages.text: Frida Kahlo’s illustrated journal brings together paintings, poems, dreams and personal reflections from the final decade of her life. Its pages move between her relationship with Diego Rivera, political concerns and the ways she expressed physical pain through images and language. An introduction by Carlos Fuentes and commentary by Sarah M. Lowe help place these intimate records in context. Reproductions, translations and photographs make the book both a visual encounter with Kahlo’s creative process and a record of her private thoughts.

pages.title: Theories of developmental psychology
pages.author: Patricia H. Miller
pages.sourceName: National Library of Medicine — fifth-edition contents
pages.text: Patricia H. Miller compares major explanations of how children develop, asking what changes, how change happens and how biology and experience interact. This fifth edition examines Piaget, Freud, Erikson and Vygotsky alongside social learning, information processing and evolutionary approaches. Chapters connect theoretical assumptions with research methods, applications and criticisms. The resulting comparison helps students distinguish between competing accounts of development instead of treating developmental psychology as a single agreed explanation.

pages.title: The 8th Habit
pages.author: Stephen R. Covey
pages.text: Stephen R. Covey extends the ideas of The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People into questions of purpose, contribution and leadership. His central proposal is to discover a personal voice and help other people develop theirs. He connects this approach with the demands of organizations in which knowledge, initiative and commitment matter. The book presents a framework for moving beyond efficient habits toward meaningful work and for considering how individual strengths can contribute to shared aims.

pages.title: Infotopia
pages.author: Cass R. Sunstein
pages.text: Cass R. Sunstein asks when a group can produce better knowledge than its individual members and when collective discussion makes mistakes worse. He examines the pressure to agree, the repetition of shared assumptions and the isolation of people from inconvenient evidence. Wikis, open-source collaboration and prediction markets provide contrasting ways of bringing information together. Infotopia explores how organizations and communities might design decisions that draw on dispersed knowledge without simply following the crowd.

pages.title: Witches
pages.author: Michael Jordan
pages.text: Michael Jordan surveys witchcraft, paganism and magic in an illustrated reference book, with photographs by Sally Griffyn. Its encyclopedic approach gives readers a way to explore related beliefs and practices by subject, while interviews bring contemporary practitioners into the discussion. The book is useful as a cultural introduction to the terminology and traditions associated with these subjects. It presents a field of religious and magical belief rather than a fictional story about witches.

pages.title: People kill people
pages.author: Ellen Hopkins
pages.text: Over one tense week, the lives of six teenagers move toward a fatal act of violence. Personal conflicts unfold within a town divided by political and racial tensions, bringing young people with different experiences into increasingly close contact. Ellen Hopkins uses the intersecting stories to examine prejudice, relationships and access to firearms. The novel builds its suspense around how ordinary decisions and accumulated pressures can converge, inviting readers to consider the people behind a public argument about violence.

pages.title: Wolfsong
pages.author: T. J. Klune
pages.text: Ox Matheson’s quiet life changes when the Bennett family moves next door. Their loyalty draws him in, but the family also carries a secret: they are werewolves. His bond with Joe, the youngest Bennett, develops against a background of belonging, violence and separation. When Joe returns after years away, Ox must confront what still connects them. The opening Green Creek novel combines an adult love story with the obligations and fractures of a found family.

pages.title: Size 14 Is Not Fat Either
pages.author: Meg Cabot
pages.text: Heather Wells expects the usual problems in her job as an assistant residence hall director at New York College. Instead, the discovery of a cheerleader’s severed head in the Fischer Hall cafeteria draws her into another murder investigation. Everyday campus responsibilities become entangled with a mystery that is much harder to manage than roommate disputes. This second Heather Wells novel continues Meg Cabot’s combination of an amateur detective, college life and a comic narrative voice.

pages.title: Spoon-Fed
pages.author: Tim Spector
pages.text: Tim Spector examines familiar claims about eating, from the importance of breakfast to calorie counting and the reputation of coffee. He questions the evidence behind diet plans, food marketing and broad nutritional rules, arguing that readers should reconsider assumptions they may have taken for granted. The book connects individual food choices with larger questions about health and the environment. Its focus is a critical discussion of nutrition research and advice rather than a single meal plan.

pages.title: Ararat
pages.author: Frank Westerman
pages.text: Frank Westerman travels toward Mount Ararat, the mountain associated with the biblical story of Noah’s Ark. Encounters with geologists, religious figures and people searching for the Ark’s remains turn the climb into an investigation of belief and evidence. Personal reflection meets the region’s political and cultural history as he considers what science can explain and why religious stories endure. This English translation by Sam Garrett combines travel writing with an inquiry into the relationship between faith and doubt.

pages.title: Always and Forever, Lara Jean
pages.author: Jenny Han
pages.text: Lara Jean is enjoying her final year at school with Peter while helping prepare for her father’s wedding. Yet choosing a college means deciding how far she is willing to move from the people and routines she loves. Plans that once seemed straightforward become harder to reconcile with her relationship and her own hopes. The third To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before novel follows the uncertainty of growing up when loyalty, ambition and first love point in different directions.

pages.title: Master and Apprentice (Star Wars)
pages.author: Claudia Gray
pages.text: Qui-Gon Jinn and his apprentice Obi-Wan Kenobi travel to Pijal to help resolve a political dispute, while doubts about their partnership remain unresolved. Qui-Gon’s interest in ancient prophecies troubles Obi-Wan, and an invitation to the Jedi Council could separate them. Deception at the royal court and visions of disaster turn the mission into a test of trust. Claudia Gray’s Star Wars novel examines what a teacher owes a student when their beliefs pull them apart.

pages.title: Faust
pages.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
pages.text: Dissatisfied with the limits of scholarship, Faust enters a dangerous bargain with Mephistopheles in pursuit of a fuller experience of life. His hunger for knowledge and fulfilment becomes inseparable from questions about temptation, responsibility and the harm his choices can cause. Goethe tells the story as a dramatic poem rather than a conventional novel. This German Library volume brings together Parts One and Two in English, edited by Victor Lange, offering the broader shape of Faust’s restless search.

pages.title: Code Name Verity
pages.author: Elizabeth Wein
pages.text: Captured in enemy territory during the Second World War, a British agent known as Verity is ordered to write a confession. Her account reaches back to her friendship with Maddie, the pilot of the plane in which they arrived. As interrogation shapes what she puts on paper, the act of telling the story becomes a struggle over survival, loyalty and truth. Elizabeth Wein’s novel combines wartime suspense with the changing meaning of a close friendship under extreme pressure.

pages.title: Somebody's Daughter
pages.author: Ashley C. Ford
pages.text: Ashley C. Ford revisits a childhood in Indiana shaped by poverty, a difficult relationship with her mother and the absence of an imprisoned father. Growing up means trying to understand the people she depends on while finding language for painful experiences of her own. The memoir explores how incarceration affects a family beyond prison walls and how an imagined parent can differ from the person eventually understood. Ford’s personal history connects questions of belonging, vulnerability and self-definition.

pages.title: Discipline Equals Freedom
pages.author: Jocko Willink
pages.text: Jocko Willink presents personal discipline as a foundation for acting on goals instead of waiting for motivation. Short discussions address fear, procrastination and the habits that can interrupt consistent effort. The book also sets out his approach to physical training, routines and preparation. Written in the direct style of a field manual, it brings together a philosophy of responsibility and practical examples of how the author applies it to everyday decisions.

pages.title: The Horse and His Boy
pages.author: C. S. Lewis
pages.text: Shasta and the talking horse Bree escape from Calormen, hoping to reach the freedom of Narnia. Their journey brings them together with Aravis and her horse, and the travellers become caught up in a danger extending beyond their own escape. C. S. Lewis tells an adventure of uncertain identities, unexpected help and learning to trust companions. Set within the world of Narnia, the story approaches that world through characters travelling toward it rather than children arriving from England.

pages.title: Genesis
pages.author: Karin Slaughter
pages.text: Sara Linton hopes her move to Atlanta will leave the past behind, until a badly injured young woman arrives in the emergency room. Will Trent’s investigation uncovers evidence of captivity and the possibility of more victims. Working with Faith Mitchell, he follows a case that brings professional tensions and private wounds into the same dangerous territory. This third Will Trent novel joins a search for a violent offender with the relationships and histories of the people pursuing him.

pages.title: Cat and Mouse
pages.author: James Patterson
pages.text: Alex Cross faces renewed danger from Gary Soneji, an escaped prisoner determined to settle a personal score. At the same time, another killer is being pursued by the formidable investigator Thomas Augustine Pierce. The two investigations create a story of rivalry, calculated attacks and uncertainty about who controls the chase. As the danger reaches Cross’s own home, James Patterson turns the detective’s professional judgment and personal vulnerability into competing pressures within the same case.

pages.title: 16 Lighthouse Road
pages.author: Debbie Macomber
pages.text: In Cedar Cove, family court judge Olivia Lockhart makes an unusual decision when a young couple’s request for divorce seems driven by grief rather than the end of love. Her ruling attracts local attention, including the interest of newspaper editor Jack Griffin. Meanwhile, family and friends have opinions about Olivia’s own life. Debbie Macomber’s opening Cedar Cove story follows a community in which private difficulties, new relationships and the possibility of second chances continually overlap.

pages.title: The Trouble with Islam Today
pages.author: Irshad Manji
pages.text: Irshad Manji writes from within her own experience of Muslim faith to argue for religious questioning and reform. Combining personal reflection with a polemical open letter, she challenges pressures against dissent and asks how believers can respond to injustice carried out in religion’s name. The book presents Manji’s particular position in a contested debate, inviting readers to examine the relationship between belief, freedom of expression and responsibility for change.

pages.title: 3rd Degree
pages.author: James Patterson
pages.text: An explosion in San Francisco draws Lindsay Boxer into an investigation marked by cryptic messages and a disturbing pattern of murders. She turns to the other members of the Women’s Murder Club as the threat moves closer to their own lives. Claire’s forensic expertise, Jill’s legal perspective and Cindy’s reporting become part of the search for a motive. James Patterson and Andrew Gross build this third series instalment around the pressure of an approaching deadline and a danger aimed at the investigators themselves.

pages.title: Double Cross
pages.author: James Patterson
pages.text: A series of elaborately staged murders brings Alex Cross and detective Brianna Stone into a case driven by a killer’s appetite for attention. Washington becomes the setting for increasingly public acts of violence, while media interest adds another layer to the offender’s performance. Cross has to understand the purpose behind the spectacle before the next attack. This Alex Cross thriller builds tension through the relationship between investigation, publicity and an adversary intent on becoming notorious.

pages.title: Ash Princess
pages.author: Laura Sebastian
pages.text: Theodosia has spent years as a captive in the palace that once belonged to her family, forced to live under the humiliating title of Ash Princess. Surviving the occupying ruler’s court has required silence and submission, but another act of cruelty makes endurance alone impossible. With little direct power, she must consider how intelligence, alliances and deception might serve resistance. Laura Sebastian’s opening fantasy novel explores the costs of reclaiming a name, a kingdom and the ability to act.

pages.title: The Physician
pages.author: Noah Gordon
pages.text: In the eleventh century, Robert Jeremy Cole journeys from England toward Persia in pursuit of medical knowledge. His ambition leads him to the school of Avicenna in Ispahan, where learning demands that he cross cultural and religious boundaries as well as physical distances. Noah Gordon combines a young man’s development with a historical world in which healing, belief and social position are closely connected. The novel opens the Cole trilogy’s long view of a family drawn to medicine.

pages.title: De orde van de dag
pages.author: Éric Vuillard
pages.text: Éric Vuillard belicht de opkomst van het nazisme via ontmoetingen en beslissingen achter de officiële beelden van macht. Van de steun van Duitse industriëlen in 1933 verschuift de aandacht naar de annexatie van Oostenrijk in 1938. Zijn korte historische vertelling onderzoekt hoe eigenbelang, intimidatie en toegeeflijkheid elkaar versterken. Met een ironische blik op bestuurders en zakenlieden doorbreekt hij het beeld van een onvermijdelijke, vlekkeloos uitgevoerde opmars. Liesbeth van Nes vertaalde het boek in het Nederlands.

pages.title: The Secret Place
pages.author: Tana French
pages.text: A year after a teenage boy is found dead at a girls’ boarding school, Holly Mackey brings detective Stephen Moran a new clue: a card from an anonymous noticeboard claiming knowledge of the murder. Moran works with Antoinette Conway to reopen the investigation. Rival friendships and guarded loyalties make the school difficult to read, while Holly’s father watches the case closely. Tana French’s Dublin Murder Squad novel explores the power of a close group and the secrets it protects.

identity.title: The Essential Ageless Body, Timeless Mind
identity.author: Deepak Chopra

pages.title: The Essential Ageless Body, Timeless Mind
pages.author: Deepak Chopra
pages.text: Deepak Chopra presents a compact introduction to his philosophy of the relationship between mind, body and ageing. He asks readers to reconsider whether identity is limited to physical appearance, established habits and familiar expectations about growing older. The book brings together reflections on awareness and personal change within his broader approach to wellbeing. Its central interest is how beliefs shape a person’s experience of life and age, offering a short entry point into Chopra’s perspective.

identity.title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
identity.author: John C. Bogle

pages.title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
pages.author: John C. Bogle
pages.text: John C. Bogle explains his case for investing through broadly diversified, low-cost index funds. He examines how fees, trading costs, taxes and attempts to time the market can reduce the returns investors receive. Rather than concentrating on selecting a winning manager or stock, the book directs attention to the costs and structure of an investment approach. This is Bogle’s argument for indexing and patient participation in markets, presented as an introduction to the reasoning behind his investment philosophy.

pages.title: Dirty
pages.author: Megan Hart
pages.text: Elle keeps her relationships at a distance, believing that control can protect her from being hurt. Meeting Dan unsettles that arrangement: attraction begins to demand a degree of trust she has worked hard to avoid. As he challenges the version of herself she presents to others, memories she has tried to contain become harder to ignore. Megan Hart’s adult romance centres on the tension between physical intimacy and emotional vulnerability, with the past shaping what connection might become possible.

identity.title: Letters from Women Who Love Too Much
identity.author: Robin Norwood

pages.title: Letters from Women Who Love Too Much
pages.author: Robin Norwood
pages.text: Robin Norwood responds to readers of Women Who Love Too Much, using their letters to examine destructive relationships and the difficulties of recovery. Correspondents describe patterns involving dependency, abuse, substance use and the fear of leaving a painful attachment. Her responses connect individual accounts with the ideas introduced in the earlier book, while a closing section includes letters from men. The question-and-response format gives the discussion a personal focus, showing how readers interpret and challenge those ideas in their own lives.

pages.title: Pucking Around
pages.author: Emily Rath
pages.text: Rachel Price arrives at the Jacksonville Rays with a sports medicine fellowship and a strong reason to keep her professional life uncomplicated. One player, however, is the man from an encounter she thought belonged in the past. An equipment manager and a superstitious goalie further unsettle the boundaries she has planned. Emily Rath’s adult hockey romance follows Rachel as attraction to more than one person challenges her assumptions about commitment, belonging and the relationships she is prepared to pursue.

pages.title: Boom
pages.author: Michael Shnayerson
pages.text: Michael Shnayerson follows the dealers who helped turn contemporary art into an international market of extraordinary prices and influence. Figures including Larry Gagosian, David Zwirner, Arne Glimcher and Iwan Wirth connect the stories of artists, galleries and collectors. The narrative moves through changing centres of the New York art world while examining partnerships, rivalries and the business of building reputations. It asks how taste, access and financial power together shape the value assigned to art.

pages.title: FAGGOTS
pages.author: Larry Kramer
pages.sourceName: Google Books — Grove Press work synopsis
pages.text: Approaching forty, Fred Lemish wants a lasting relationship but finds himself moving through a social world dominated by appearance, status and sexual opportunity. Larry Kramer uses Fred’s search to construct a confrontational satire of gay life in 1970s New York. The novel’s adult subject matter and deliberately abrasive humour accompany a question about whether constant pursuit leaves room for intimacy. It presents one writer’s critical vision of a particular milieu, with longing for connection beneath the social comedy.
